question.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=5$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-x+30?$
question.worked_solution:
Since $x=5$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-5)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-5)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-5)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $5$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $-1$ | $30$ |
|  | $↓$ | $5$ | $-5$ | $-30$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-5}={x}^{2}-x-6,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-5)({x}^{2}-x-6).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-5)(x-3)(x+2).\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $1.$
